That’s a great place to start — and honestly, a balcony garden is a perfect “first project,” especially if you’ve already absorbed some of it over the years.

Morning sun with afternoon shade is actually quite workable. It’s not ideal for every vegetable, but plenty will do just fine.

Tomatoes are the one to think about carefully. They really prefer full sun (6–8 hours), so on a morning-only balcony they’ll grow, but you might get fewer fruits and slower progress. If you’d like to try them anyway, go for a small or “patio” variety — things like cherry tomatoes tend to be more forgiving.

Herbs, on the other hand, are a very safe bet and usually thrive in those conditions. Good choices for your setup:
- Basil (does well with morning sun, just keep it watered)
- Parsley (very forgiving)
- Chives (almost hard to mess up)
- Mint (grows vigorously — best in its own pot so it doesn’t take over)
- Thyme or oregano (like a bit of sun but don’t mind some shade)

If you want a vegetable that’s easier than tomatoes in partial sun, consider:
- Lettuce or salad greens (they actually prefer less intense sun)
- Spinach
- Radishes (quick and satisfying)

A couple of simple tips that make a big difference:
- Use pots with drainage holes — very important
- Good potting soil (not garden soil)
- Water regularly, since containers dry out faster than ground soil
- If your balcony gets breezy, keep that in mind — it can dry plants quickly

If you’d like, I can suggest a very simple “starter setup” — just a few pots and plants to get you going without much fuss.

On the parsley: yellowing leaves are usually a sign that something’s a bit off, but it’s often an easy fix. The most common cause in pots is actually too much water rather than too little — even when you’re being careful.

A couple of things to check:

First, after you water, does excess water drain out the bottom of the pot? If it doesn’t, the roots can end up sitting in water, which parsley doesn’t like.

Second, when you check the soil, make sure you’re not just feeling the very top. The surface can dry out quickly, but underneath may still be quite damp. If it’s still moist an inch down, give it another day before watering.

A simple way to read the plant itself:
- Yellow leaves + soft stems = often too much water
- Yellow leaves + dry, brittle feel = usually too little water

Also, don’t worry if it’s just some of the older, lower leaves turning yellow — parsley will naturally cycle those out as it grows.

A small adjustment you could try: let the soil dry just a little more between waterings for the parsley compared to the basil. Basil tends to be thirstier.

If the pot has good drainage, you’re using potting mix, and you ease up slightly on watering, it will likely settle down.

One more minor point — parsley doesn’t need quite as much sun as basil, so if it’s in the exact same spot, that’s fine, but it wouldn’t mind a slightly shadier position if that’s an option.

You’re doing the right things. This is exactly the stage where you start to get a feel for what each plant prefers — a bit like what your wife used to say about plants “telling you” what they need. This is how that starts to make sense.
